title: Subnet masks, CIDR and calculating hosts per range

videos.script: A network called ten, twenty, thirty-two, zero, slash twenty-four. In this lab it is cut into three LANs of different sizes, behind one router. {{plan}} Every machine on them has a mask, and the mask decides one thing every time it sends a packet: is this destination on my cable, or does it go to the gateway? {{decision}} This lesson is the arithmetic behind that decision. First the mask in binary: a row of ones, then zeros, and the AND that turns an address into its network. {{and}} Then the short way to write a mask, the slash and a number, which replaced the old classes in 1993. {{prefix}} Then the two ends of every range, and how many machines fit between them. Two less than you might think. {{hosts}} Then a method that does all of it in your head, in a few seconds, checked against a calculator. {{by-hand}} Last, one wrong number typed into one machine. The internet still works from it. The server two cables away does not. You will see exactly why, in the machine's own tables. {{wrong-mask}}
